To proceed, CJCs must clearly articulate how their chosen sectoral cluster can support the programmes objectives. This must include, at a minimum, how the Investment Zone will do at least one of the following:

boost productivity in the region

increase real earnings for high and low skilled workers within the region

increase international competitiveness of companies within the cluster

internationally demanded new technologies

Reduce emissions on a local or regional scale

Research institution co-sign

Considering the focus of your Investment Zone, which research institution(s) will co-sign your Investment Zone proposal? (250 words)

CJCs must identify a research institution(s) to be a co-signatory of the document, setting out why they are appropriate to do so based on the priority sector, the needs of the cluster and wider area.

To proceed to the next Gateway, CJCs must identify and name their co-signatory partner(s) research institution.

Gateway 3: Governance

Governance Question 1

Set out if the governance structure that will oversee the Investment Zone is existing or not? (750 words)

If No:

set out the proposed Governance structures and provide detail on how this will achieve Investment Zone objectives. CJCs must evidence interim structures as the proposed structures are developed

where setting up new governance, CJCs should set out why new governance is needed, clear and implementable milestones for its formation and the proposed membership and frequency of meetings during design and delivery of the programme

If Yes:

provide documentation to evidence the current structure, membership and how it will be able to consider the specific sector and innovation considerations of the Investment Zone

if using an existing governance structure, CJCs should provide existing membership, proof of track record of delivery and how it has been adapted or will bring in sector/cluster experience

CJCs must ensure governance structures draw on the expertise needed to grow their cluster, with a clear link to the priority sector and its needs

the proposed governance structure should engage the research institutions, innovation eco-system and could consider how to involve other partners, such as:

sector specific businesses

supply chain businesses

wider research institutions, for example, Catapults

cluster bodies

education, skills providers, employment experts and providers

To proceed, CJCs must have strong existing governance in place or a clear and implementable plan to form new governance. This should be supported by evidence requested. Governments will consider if the governance structures appropriately engage cluster expertise from the sector, wider research institutions and stakeholders.

Governance Question 2

What is the team structure for design and delivery of the Investment Zone proposal? (500 words, plus file)

CJCs must set out the proposed management arrangements for design and delivery of Investment Zone. CJCs should describe the accountability and assurance that will be in place for design and delivery of the Investment Zone, if this uses existing structures, CJCs should detail arrangements here. CJCs must provide the following evidence:

a named senior responsible officer for the Investment Zone, listing their responsibilities and accountabilities throughout the stages of the Investment Zone

details and description of the planned team to oversee the Investment Zone, including timelines for appointments or details about existing structures, if in place

This should be provided in one of several formats:

organogram

list of roles and responsibilities

if proposing tax or NDR retention sites, it must include specific details on their planned future management

To proceed to the next gateway, CJCs must provide the evidence requested, which will be considered based on its credibility.

Governance Question 3

How will relevant research institutions and other stakeholders be engaged and involved in the Investment Zone Governance? (500 words)

CJCs should set out how partner organisations will feed into the process of Investment design and delivery. The Welsh Government and UK Government will want to work with CJCs to ensure proposals have clear plans and to engage relevant organisations, to consider what direct support they can offer to an Investment Zone proposal. Proposals should consider how they can be leveraged to secure direct support they can offer to an Investment Zone proposal.

Governance proposals must engage research institutions and other stakeholders beyond the simple co-sign of the research institution above. The programme governance must ensure they have a long-term role to inform delivery and bring to bear their own resources.

Governance Question 4

How will you engage Planning Authorities as you develop and deliver the planning offer as part of Investment Zones? (250 words)

CJCs should explain the engagement to date with Planning Authorities and how that has informed the design of their Investment Zone proposal and how it will enable future delivery. CJCs should also set out how they have engaged Strategic Development Plans and Regional Transport Plans.

CJCs ought to engage with Local Planning Authorities and provide evidence that any planning requirements ensure alignment with existing plans including Future Wales The National Plan 2040 and adopted local development plans

To proceed, Investment Zone proposals must:

evidence engagement with the relevant Planning Authorities

Planning

Planning objectives

Developments must be in accordance with Future Wales The National Plan 2040, the relevant local development plan for the area and Planning Policy Wales. Areas should look to best practice and follow innovative approaches where they would add value. This should include commencing work on Strategic Development Plans in parallel with work on Regional Transport Plans. The establishment of project-focussed teams, including major application teams, proactive master-planning, use of planning protocols or processing agreements and aligning consent procedures where appropriate is encouraged.

We envisage each area using their core Investment Zone funding to support this planning offer.

We expect planning interventions to contribute to physical intermediate outcomes as development sites are unlocked at a faster rate (and at a higher quality) through these activities to speed up the planning process.

upskilling planners/ procuring consultants/employing additional resource to develop a masterplan for the regeneration of new city quarter.

employing a dedicated planning lead at the CJC level who can unblock issues and drive proactive engagement (inc. with developers)

CJCs should also consider and implement wherever possible:

sustainability and green measures in procurement plans, aligned with the climate adaptation plan

Fair work, aligned with the approach set out in A guide to fair work

publication of advance contract pipelines of planned contracts to provide local business with confidence and certainty to invest in skills development and be ready to compete as contracts are advertised

collaboration with other stakeholders managing other planned investment and expenditure outside of the Investment Zones programme. Such collaboration could explore approaches to ensure that local business capacity and skills are not swamped as a result of peaks in demand for similar services, supplies and/or works

innovative procurement, including the factoring in of social value (or Well-being outcomes in Wales) into procurement and strategies to engage Foundational Economy businesses

UK government initiatives, guidance and policy such as the Sourcing and Consultancy Playbooks, Construction Playbook, the Outsourcing Playbook and government guidance on Resolution Planning, or equivalent materials in Wales, for example the Social Public Workforce and Outsourcing Code in Wales.

It will be the responsibility of the CJC and its accountable body to ensure that minimum standards stated above are applied proportionately, monitored, and maintained throughout the period of the Investment Zones grant.

Where non-contracting authorities are involved in Investment Zones project delivery, they should adopt such policies and procedures that are required to ensure that value for money has been obtained in the procurement of goods or services funded by the programme. This should include adopting the following minimum procedures unless different thresholds have been approved internally via the accountable body’s appropriate internal governance process and their Chief Finance Officer:

if the value of contract is £0 - £2,499 then the minimum procedure is to directly award

if the value of contract is £2,500 - £24,999 then the minimum procedure is three written quotes or prices sought from relevant suppliers of goods, works and / or services

if the value of the contract us over £25,000 then the minimum procedure is a formal tender process

Accountable bodies will be responsible for ensuring that these policies and procedures are applied by non-contracting authorities as appropriate, reported upon and monitored.

Fraud Risk Assessment (FRA)

Accountable bodies shall be responsible for ensuring that fraud is a key consideration in all spend activity and that the following minimum standards are met:

meet Grants Functional Standard on Fraud Risk Assessment (FRA) – pages 15-19

undertake FRAs at an appropriate level to each individual project dependent on risk

ensure that Investment Zones spend is undertaken in accordance with effective authority fraud prevention policy and procedure, and via engagement with colleagues specialising in this area

ensure that relevant evidence and data to prevent fraud is gathered as part of due diligence undertaken ahead of releasing funds

implement reporting and monitoring requirements that will identify irregularities or issues in use of funds which can be investigated further

store and file all work undertaken on FRA in the event of any issues or audit requirements

Due diligence

Accountable bodies shall be responsible for ensuring that proportional due diligence is applied to all Investment Zones spend and that the following minimum standards are met:

meet Grants Functional Standard on Due Diligence – pages 20-24

undertake due diligence at an appropriate level to each individual project dependent on risk

ensure that Investment Zones due diligence is undertaken in accordance with effective authority rules and procedures through teams specialising in this area

ensure that key areas of due diligence identified for projects in which you invest are reported on and monitored throughout the term of delivery

store and file all work undertaken on due diligence in the event of any issues or audit requirements

In Wales, the monitoring and accountability requirements in the Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023.

9. Equalities

In Great Britain, the public sector equality duty (PSED) under the Equality Act 2010 (“Act”) requires public authorities in exercising their functions to have due regard to the need to: eliminate discrimination, harassment, victimisation, and any other conduct that is prohibited by or under the Act; advance equality of opportunity between persons who share a relevant protected characteristic and persons who do not share it; foster good relations between persons who share a relevant protected characteristic and persons who do not share it.

Accountable bodies in Great Britain are required to comply with PSED when carrying out their duties related to the Investment Zones.

As part of PSED, the UK Government will conduct a programme level equality impact assessment with Welsh Government requiring CJCs to conduct a region level equality impact assessment on Investment Zones after proposals have finalised and the types of interventions to be delivered for each region are known. Accountable bodies will be responsible for their own compliance with the PSED duties.

10. Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015

In Wales, the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (‘the Act’) provides the context within which public bodies, including CJCs, must exercise their functions. CJCs must use their resources and ensure their governance is effective with the aim of maximising their contribution to Wales’ national well-being goals.
